section.title: AI & Mathematics
section.label: Section One
section.description: The vocabulary of machine learning, statistics, optimisation and the linear algebra underneath all of it. Every entry is defined in terms a reader can substitute back into a sentence, then anchored to the paper or theorem it came from.

definitions.text: an iterative procedure that reduces a differentiable objective by repeatedly stepping in the direction opposite to its slope at the current point.
definitions.example: Training halted once gradient descent stopped lowering the validation objective.

definitions.text: the family of training algorithms that update model parameters from the slope of a loss surface, including the stochastic and mini-batch variants used in practice.
definitions.example: Nearly every deep network in production was fitted by some form of gradient descent.

formula.note: eta is the step size, or learning rate; grad J is the slope of the objective at the current parameters.

entries.etymology: From gradient, Latin gradiens 'stepping', plus descent, Old French descente 'a going down'. Named for the geometric picture of walking downhill on a surface.

citations.label: Cauchy, A. (1847). Méthode générale pour la résolution des systèmes d'équations simultanées.
citations.source: Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, 25, 536–538.

citations.label: Robbins, H. & Monro, S. (1951). A Stochastic Approximation Method.

definitions.text: an application of the chain rule that computes the sensitivity of a loss to every parameter in a layered network by passing partial derivatives from the output back toward the input.
definitions.example: One backpropagation pass yields every parameter's derivative in roughly the cost of one forward pass.

formula.plain: dL/dW(l) = delta(l) * a(l-1)^T,  delta(l) = W(l+1)^T * delta(l+1) .* sigma'(z(l))
formula.note: delta is the error signal at a layer; the circled dot is elementwise multiplication.

entries.etymology: A 1980s contraction of 'backward propagation of errors'. Popularised by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams in 1986, though the underlying reverse-mode differentiation was described by Linnainmaa in 1970.

citations.label: Rumelhart, D., Hinton, G. & Williams, R. (1986). Learning representations by back-propagating errors.
Linnainmaa, S. (1970). The representation of the cumulative rounding error of an algorithm as a Taylor expansion of the local rounding errors.

definitions.text: the failure mode in which a model absorbs noise particular to its training sample and therefore predicts unseen data worse than a simpler model would.
definitions.example: Validation error rose while training error kept falling — textbook overfitting.

formula.note: Overfitting is the regime where the variance term dominates the decomposition.

entries.etymology: From over- 'excessively' plus fit, in the statistical sense of fitting a curve to points; in use in the regression literature from the mid-twentieth century.

citations.label: Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R. & Friedman, J. (2009). The Elements of Statistical Learning, ch. 7.

definitions.text: a non-zero vector whose direction is unchanged by a given linear map, so the map merely rescales it by a constant factor.
definitions.example: The covariance matrix's leading eigenvector points along the axis of greatest spread in the data.

formula.note: lambda is the eigenvalue: the factor by which the map stretches that direction.

entries.etymology: A partial calque of German Eigenvektor, from eigen 'own, characteristic'. Hilbert used Eigenwert in 1904; the hybrid German-English form settled into English mathematics in the 1920s–30s.

citations.label: Strang, G. (2016). Introduction to Linear Algebra, 5th ed., ch. 6.

definitions.text: a layer that produces each output as a weighted blend of all available inputs, where the weights are computed from the similarity between a query and a set of keys.
definitions.example: The attention mechanism let the decoder consult any source token instead of a single fixed summary vector.

formula.note: Division by sqrt(d_k) keeps the dot products in a range where softmax gradients do not vanish.

entries.etymology: Borrowed from cognitive psychology, where attention names the selective allocation of processing. Introduced to neural machine translation by Bahdanau et al. in 2014.

citations.label: Bahdanau, D., Cho, K. & Bengio, Y. (2015). Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate.
Vaswani, A. et al. (2017). Attention Is All You Need.

definitions.text: the identity that converts the likelihood of evidence given a hypothesis into the probability of the hypothesis given that evidence, by weighting it with the hypothesis's prior probability.
definitions.example: Applying Bayes' theorem to a positive test result requires the disease's base rate, not just the test's accuracy.

formula.note: P(A) is the prior, P(B|A) the likelihood, P(A|B) the posterior.

entries.etymology: An eponym (Rule 519) after Thomas Bayes (c. 1701–1761), the English Presbyterian minister whose essay on the problem was published posthumously by Richard Price in 1763.

citations.label: Bayes, T. & Price, R. (1763). An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances.
citations.source: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 53, 370–418.
